title: Unit 2 Overview: Linear (1D) Processing and Data Storage
summary: Overview slide placing Unit 2 (Linear/1D Processing) in context among the course's four units, now raising the question of how to store linear datasets, which motivates arrays.
main_text: This slide repeats the course roadmap from Unit 2b: Unit 1 covers Scalar processing (IPO: Input-Process-Output programs); Unit 2, the current unit, covers Linear (1D) Processing; Unit 3 covers Multidimensional Processing; and Unit 4 covers Divide & Conquer (Functional Decomposition). New to this version of the slide is an orange annotation next to the Unit 2 diagram asking 'How do we store these data sets,' explicitly motivating the need for arrays as the data structure used to hold linear (1D) collections of values, which is the focus of this unit (2c).
notes_text: The added callout 'How do we store these data sets' is the key transition from Unit 2b (writing loops) into Unit 2c (arrays), framing arrays as the missing piece needed to actually hold the data that loops process.

images.description: Four stacked diagrams showing increasing complexity: scalar (single value) through a processor, linear (1D array) through a processor with an orange annotation asking how such data sets are stored, multidimensional (2D grid) through a processor, and a functional decomposition box with f(x) and g(y).
labels: How do we store these data sets

title: Motivating Example
summary: Uses the problem of storing many students' grades to motivate arrays, contrasting the manageable case of 3-4 separate variables with the impractical case of 140 separately-named variables.
main_text: This slide motivates the need for arrays with a concrete scenario: storing the grades for all students in a class so statistics can be computed, the grades sorted, printed, and so on. Each grade needs to be stored in a variable that can be accessed and used later. With only 3 or 4 students, this is easy — the example shows int score1, score2, score3; read via cin, then compared with nested if conditions to determine the smallest. However, with many students (the example scales to 140), this approach becomes painful: the code shown declares 140 separately named variables (score1 through score140) and reads them all in individually via a long chain of cin >> statements, illustrating how unmanageable and repetitive this becomes without a way to group related data under one name and access it via an index.
notes_text: This slide sets up the core motivation for arrays: avoiding the need to declare hundreds of individually-named variables for related data.

title: Control vs. Data Structures
summary: Distinguishes control structures (if, while, for) from data structures, introducing arrays as the simplest data structure and the only one natively supported by C/C++.
main_text: This slide draws a distinction between two categories of language constructs. Control structures are language constructs that allow programs to make decisions; common examples are if statements, while loops, and for loops (all covered in Unit 2b). Separately, programs also need ways to store data so it can be accessed easily and efficiently — this is the role of data structures. Arrays are introduced as the simplest data structure, and notably the only one that C/C++ supports natively (built into the language itself). Other data structures (such as vectors, lists, or maps) are available only through additional library code, whereas arrays require no additional includes or libraries to use.

title: Computer Memory: Array Basics
summary: Defines an array as a named, ordered, same-type collection of variables stored contiguously in memory and accessed via an index, illustrated with a 140-element scores array.
main_text: An array is defined as a named collection of ordered variables of the same type that are accessed with an index and stored contiguously in memory. Four defining properties are broken down: (1) Named collection — one name refers to the entire collection of variables; (2) Ordered — there is a first and a last element, with a defined sequence between them; (3) Accessed with an index — each variable is accessed via its position/index using square bracket [] notation; (4) Same type — all variables in one array must share the same type (e.g., an array cannot mix doubles and ints). A memory diagram shows an array named scores with elements at indices [0], [1], [2], ..., [139], each stored at consecutive memory addresses (520, 524, 528, ..., 1076), incrementing by 4 bytes per int element. The accompanying code declares int scores[140]; performing a one-time allocation of 140 integers (initially containing garbage/undefined values), then uses a for loop (for(int i=0; i<140; i++) cin >> scores[i];) to read in all 140 values one at a time via their index. A key note: once allocated, only one element can be accessed at a time via its index.
notes_text: The memory diagram explicitly shows addresses incrementing by 4 bytes per element (520, 524, 528, ...), reinforcing that arrays are stored contiguously in memory.

images.description: Memory layout diagram showing a 140-element integer array named 'scores', with each index (0 through 139) mapped to a specific contiguous memory address (520, 524, 528, ..., 1076), each 4 bytes apart, holding example values like 96, 84, 93, ..., 90.

title: Accessing An Element
summary: Explains how to access an individual array element using square-bracket indexing with any valid expression that evaluates to a legal index (0 to n-1), with worked examples.
main_text: Once an array is declared, there is nothing 'special' about it — each element/variable must still be initialized and accessed one at a time. To access an individual element of an array of size n, the array's name is followed by square brackets containing ANY expression (a constant, variable, or arithmetic expression) that evaluates to an index from 0 to n-1; indexing starts at 0. Worked examples using int scores[10]; (allocating 10 integers) and int x=1, myval=5;: scores[4] = 73; directly sets index 4; scores[x] = 82; sets scores[1] since x equals 1; scores[2*x + 1] = 93; sets scores[3] since 2*1+1=3; scores[1+max(x,myval)] = 88; sets scores[6] since max(1,5)=5 and 1+5=6. A memory diagram shows the resulting array state after these assignments: index [1]=82, [3]=93, [4]=73, [6]=88, with other indices left as undefined ('??'). The key takeaway is that the index can be generated using any legal C++ expression that evaluates to the desired index value.
notes_text: The examples deliberately mix constant, variable, and function-based (max()) index expressions to reinforce that indices are just expressions, not only literal numbers.

images.description: Memory diagram showing the resulting values of a 10-element scores array after several indexed assignment statements, with populated indices 1 (82), 3 (93), 4 (73), and 6 (88), and remaining indices shown as undefined ('??').

title: Index vs. Value
summary: Distinguishes an array index (the expression inside square brackets) from the value/data stored at that index, showing that indices can themselves be arbitrary expressions, including nested array lookups.
main_text: The expression written inside square brackets is called an index; using array[index] yields the data/value stored in the array at that index. An index can be ANY EXPRESSION, including a value read from another part of the same array or the return value of a function call. For an array declared with size n, only indices 0 through n-1 are legal. Given int scores[20]; filled with data, and int i = 1;, three example expressions are shown (with blanks for their resulting values, to be solved later on slide 23): int x = scores[2*i + 1]; (index 2*1+1=3), int y = scores[scores[1]]; (a nested index — first look up scores[1], then use that value as the index into scores again), and int z = scores[max(4,2)]; (index max(4,2)=4). A memory diagram shows the array's index positions and their corresponding stored values side by side to visualize the index vs. value distinction.
notes_text: The nested indexing example, scores[scores[1]], is a deliberately tricky illustration of using an array's own stored value as an index into itself.

images.description: Side-by-side memory diagram distinguishing an array's index positions from the values stored at those positions, for a 20-element scores array with sample values 9, 0, 7, 8, 6 shown at indices 0 through 4.

title: Loops and Arrays (1)
summary: Introduces the key power of combining loops with arrays: using the loop control variable as the array index so the same code works regardless of array size.
main_text: The real power of arrays emerges when they are combined with loops. The loop control variable (typically named i) can serve directly as the index of the array entry to be modified or accessed. This means whether the array has 1 element or 1,000,000 elements, the code size (the loop body) does not need to grow. Two examples are given using int scores[100];: the first for loop, for(int i=0; i<100; i++) { scores[i] = 0; }, initializes every element of the array to 0; the second (an alternative), for(int i=0; i<100; i++) { cin >> scores[i]; }, instead reads in all 100 entries from user input, one per iteration, using the loop variable i as the index into scores. A memory diagram shows the resulting all-zero array after the initialization loop runs.
notes_text: This is the central conceptual payoff of the unit: combining Unit 2b's loop constructs with arrays lets a fixed amount of code process arbitrarily large collections of data.

images.description: Memory diagram showing a 100-element scores array after being initialized to all zeros via a for loop, with index positions 0 through 6 shown holding the value 0.

title: When Do We Need Arrays?
summary: Clarifies that arrays are needed specifically when data must be revisited more than once, contrasting a two-pass array-based average/max computation with a simpler one-pass streaming approach that needs no array.
main_text: This slide reframes the key question: arrays CAN store many related data items of the same type, but the more important question is WHEN we NEED to store data in an array. The answer given is: arrays are needed when the data must be revisited more than once. If a task only requires finding the min/max or average, the data can instead be read from the user and the sum or min/max updated on the fly, without storing every individual data item — meaning arrays should not be introduced where they are not needed. Two contrasting code examples make this concrete: the first stores all 100 scores in an array (reading them into scores[i] in one loop, then computing the sum in a second separate loop over scores[i]) requiring two full passes over stored data; the second computes the running sum directly as each value is read (int val, sum=0; for(...) { cin >> val; sum += val; }) without ever storing the values in an array, needing only a single pass and no array at all.
notes_text: This is an important design-judgment slide: it corrects a possible over-application of arrays by clarifying that a single-pass reduction (as taught in Unit 2b) doesn't need an array — only tasks requiring multiple passes or random access to previously seen values do.

images.description: Two side-by-side C++ code blocks contrasted directly: one stores all 100 input values into a scores array across two separate loops (input then sum), the other computes a running sum in a single loop without ever storing values in an array, illustrating when an array is truly necessary versus unnecessary.
labels: Get the data & average it at the same time

title: A Common Error: Out-of-Bounds Access
summary: Warns about out-of-bounds array access (segmentation faults), showing a buggy loop that iterates one index too far and demonstrating safe vs. unsafe index usage.
main_text: Care must be taken to avoid using an index that leads to an out-of-bounds array access, since such an access will either corrupt other data or crash the program. These crashes are often known as segmentation faults, and the slide advises that the first thought upon seeing one should be to check for a bad array index. The buggy example shown declares int scores[20]; then loops for(i=0; i <= 20; i++) { scores[i] = 0; }, which is flagged as wrong because using <= together with a 20-element array causes the loop to run from i=0 to i=20 inclusive (21 iterations), writing to the illegal index scores[20], one past the valid range of 0-19. A further example shows reading an arbitrary index i from the user and directly writing scores[i] = 100; as unsafe (not guaranteed to be in bounds), contrasted with a safe version that first checks if(i >= 0 && i < 20) { scores[i] = 100; } before performing the write.
notes_text: This slide directly echoes the 'off-by-one error' warning from Unit 2b (using <= instead of < in a loop bound), now shown to have more severe consequences (crashes/corruption) when applied to array indexing rather than simple counting.

images.description: Memory diagram showing a 20-element scores array (indices 0-19) with an out-of-bounds access at index 20 highlighted as landing outside the array's allocated memory region, illustrating the consequence of an off-by-one loop bound error.

title: Important C/C++ Rule: Array Size
summary: Explains the C/C++ rule that array sizes must be known at compile time (fixed/constant), and the course convention of allocating a large fixed-size array and using only part of it.
main_text: C/C++ requires that the SIZE of an array be known at compile time, not at run time. This means the array's size must be ONE FIXED (or constant) value every time the program runs — it cannot vary based on runtime input. For this course, the recommended approach is to allocate a LARGE array sized to the maximum possible need, and then use only a portion of it as the program actually runs; future courses will teach more sophisticated (memory-efficient) ways to handle this. Example code contrasts GOOD practice — int data[24]; where 24 is a compile-time-known constant — with BAD practice — int n; cin >> n; int data[n]; where n is not known until runtime, which is illegal in standard C/C++. A correct pattern is shown: int data[100]; declares a fixed maximum-size array, then int n; cin >> n; reads how many elements are actually needed, followed by for(int i=0; i<n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } which only fills and uses the first n elements of the fixed 100-element array.

title: Initializing Arrays With Constants
summary: Explains how to initialize an array at declaration time using a brace-enclosed initializer list, including partial initialization (remaining elements default to 0) and omitting the explicit size.
main_text: Arrays can be initialized with constant values at the point of declaration using an initialization list: a comma-separated list of constants enclosed in curly braces {…}. An important exception: if fewer values are provided than the declared size of the array, the remaining elements are automatically filled with 0s. If an initialization list is provided, the array's size need not be explicitly specified in the square brackets (empty [] is sufficient), since the compiler can determine the required size by counting the number of initial values given. Examples: int data[5] = {9, 7, 8, 9, 5}; explicitly sizes the array to 5, matching the 5 given values; double dec[4] = {0.25, 0.3}; declares size 4 but only provides 2 values, so the array becomes {0.25, 0.3, 0, 0}; int nums[4] = {0}; initializes all 4 elements to 0. Alternatively, int data[] = {9, 7, 8, 9, 5}; and double dec[] = {0.25, 0.3, 0.18, 0.2}; omit the explicit size entirely, letting the compiler infer sizes of 5 and 4 respectively from the initializer lists.

title: Section Divider: Array Tasks and Access Patterns
summary: Section divider slide introducing strategies and questions for determining coding approaches to array-based tasks.
main_text: This is a section title slide reading 'ARRAY TASKS AND ACCESS PATTERNS, Strategies and questions to ask to determine coding approaches...'. It contains no additional instructional content and transitions into the discussion of sequential versus random access patterns for arrays.

title: Sequential vs. Random Access
summary: Introduces the two fundamental array access patterns: sequential access, which loops through all elements, and random access, which computes a single index to access directly.
main_text: Most array-based tasks fall into either a sequential-access pattern or a random-access pattern. Sequential access iterates (loops) through all elements of an array, and is used for tasks that require looking at all elements in the worst case; the example shown computes a running total by looping through every index of a 20-element scores array: int total = 0; for(int i=0; i<20; i++) { total += scores[i]; }. Random access instead computes the ONE index needed to access a specific element directly, without looping through the rest of the array; the example shown reads a student ID (an integer from 0-19) from the user and directly prints scores[stuID], the score belonging to that specific student, with no loop involved at all. This distinction (sequential vs. random access) is presented as a key strategic question to ask when designing array-based code.

images.description: Two side-by-side memory diagrams of the same 20-element scores array: one illustrating sequential access, where a loop visits every index from 0 to 19 to accumulate a total; the other illustrating random access, where a single computed index (a student ID between 0 and 19) is used to directly retrieve one specific score.

title: Sequential Access
summary: Details when sequential access is required, listing common task categories: combining all elements (sum, average, count-if, modify-all) and searching/selecting an element with possible early exit.
main_text: Sequential access should be used whenever a task MUST (or potentially needs to) visit EVERY element of an array. Common tasks requiring sequential access fall into two groups. The first group is combining ALL elements, including computing a sum or average, performing a count-if operation (e.g., counting how many scores equal exactly 100), or a modify-all operation (e.g., incrementing every element by some amount) — these directly correspond to the Reduce and Map idioms from Unit 2b, now applied specifically to array elements. The second group is searching for or selecting an element, potentially stopping early via a break statement (particularly relevant in an unsorted array), including finding a particular target value, or finding the minimum or maximum value — these correspond to the Selection idiom, now combined with the possibility of an early break once the target is found.
notes_text: This slide is the array-specific application of the Map, Reduce, and Selection idioms introduced in Unit 2b, now framed through the lens of which access pattern (sequential) each requires.

images.description: Two memory diagrams of a 20-element scores array illustrating sequential-access tasks: one showing a running total being accumulated across all elements (sum), and one showing a search operation looking for a specific target value (96) that may stop early once found.

title: Section Divider: Solutions
summary: Section divider slide introducing the worked solutions to earlier array exercises in the deck.
main_text: This is a section title slide reading 'SOLUTIONS.' It contains no additional instructional content and transitions into the worked solutions for the Loops and Arrays average/max exercises and the Index vs. Value exercise posed earlier in the deck.

title: Solution: Loops and Arrays (2) — Average and Max
summary: Provides the worked solution for computing both the average and the maximum of a 100-element scores array, combining the reduction and selection idioms in one program.
main_text: This slide gives the combined solution to the average and maximum exercises from slides 9 and 10. Given int scores[100]; already filled with data, the average is computed with: int sum = 0; for(int i=0; i<100; i++) { sum += scores[i]; } cout << (double)sum / 100 << endl;, using an explicit cast to double to ensure floating-point (rather than truncated integer) division. The maximum is computed with: int max = 0; for(int i=0; i<100; i++) { if(scores[i] > max) max = scores[i]; } cout << 'Max: ' << max << endl;. Both loops apply the reduction-variable (sum) and selection (max tracking) idioms from Unit 2b directly to array elements via the loop index i, sequentially visiting every element of the array.
notes_text: Note: initializing max to 0 (rather than a very small or negative sentinel value) works correctly here only because all valid scores are assumed to be non-negative; this is a subtle assumption worth flagging for students, especially since slide 22's version uses max = -1 instead.

title: Solution: Loops and Arrays (3) — Maximum Score
summary: Provides the worked solution specifically for finding the maximum score in a 100-element scores array, initializing the running max to -1 as a safe sentinel value.
main_text: This slide gives the dedicated solution to the maximum-score exercise from slide 10. Given int scores[100]; already filled with data, the maximum is computed with: int max = -1; for(int i=0; i<100; i++) { if(scores[i] > max) max = scores[i]; } cout << 'Max: ' << max << endl;. Initializing max to -1 (rather than 0, as in the previous slide's version) is a safer sentinel value here, since it correctly handles the case where all scores could be 0, ensuring the first real score encountered will always be greater than the initial max and thus properly recorded.
notes_text: This slide's max = -1 initialization is more robust than slide 21's max = 0 approach, and mirrors the same -1 sentinel pattern used for the max-finding example in the Unit 2b Selection Idiom slides.

title: Solution: Index vs. Value
summary: Provides the worked solution to the Index vs. Value exercise from slide 7, filling in the resulting values of three example indexed expressions.
main_text: This slide gives the solution to the exercise on slide 7. Given int scores[20]; filled with data and int i = 1;, the three example expressions resolve as follows: int x = scores[2*i + 1]; evaluates the index 2*1+1=3, giving x=8 (the value stored at index 3); int y = scores[scores[1]]; first looks up scores[1], which is 0, then uses that as the index, so y = scores[0] = 9; int z = scores[max(4,2)]; evaluates the index max(4,2)=4, giving z=6 (the value stored at index 4). The same memory diagram from slide 7 is repeated, now with the resolved index and value relationships fully worked out, showing scores holding values 9, 0, 7, 8, 6, ... at indices 0 through 4.

images.description: Memory diagram of a 20-element scores array with example values 9, 0, 7, 8, 6 at indices 0 through 4, annotated with the resolved results of the index-vs-value exercise: x=8, y=9, z=6.
